name: Iceland
summary: A volcanic island settled by Norse people around 874, ruled by Norway and Denmark, sovereign from 1918 and a republic since 1944.

knownFor.label: Althing
knownFor.note: One of the oldest parliaments, founded in 930.

knownFor.label: Geothermal power
knownFor.note: Heat and electricity from volcanic ground.

location.value: An island in the North Atlantic; about 103,000 km².

climate.value: Cool, wet and windy, milder than its latitude suggests thanks to the Gulf Stream; Reykjavík’s winters average around 0 °C.

resources.value: Fish, plentiful geothermal heat and hydropower; cheap green electricity attracts aluminium smelters and data centres.

population.value: About 390,000 people, the smallest population of any NATO or OECD country.

urbanisation.value: About two-thirds of people live in the Reykjavík area; the interior is almost empty.

disease.value: Very long life expectancy (about 83 years) and a universal health system.

economicBase.value: Fishing, tourism (boomed after 2010) and aluminium smelting powered by renewable energy.

tradeRoutes.value: Exports fish and aluminium by sea to Europe; Keflavík airport links it to Europe and North America.

wealth.value: One of the richest countries per person, with a strong welfare state.

moneyAndTax.value: The Icelandic króna; high taxes fund free education and health care.

inequality.value: Among the most equal countries in the world, including in pay between women and men.

governmentType.value: A parliamentary republic with an elected president; the Althing is one of the oldest parliaments in the world.

keyRulers.value: Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, the world’s first elected woman president (1980).

succession.value: Coalition governments formed after elections to the Althing.

institutions.value: The Althing, founded about 930 and restored in 1845; independent courts and strong local councils.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between the Independence Party and left-leaning parties; protests after 2008 brought down the government.

armyAndTech.value: Has no army; a coast guard and NATO membership provide defence. A US base at Keflavík operated until 2006.

majorWars.value: “Cod Wars” with Britain over fishing waters (1958–76), won by Iceland without deaths in battle.

territoryChange.value: Fishing limits extended to 200 nautical miles (1975).

alliancesRivals.value: Founding NATO member (1949); in the European Economic Area but not the EU.

inventions.value: World leader in using geothermal energy for heating; few major inventions.

scienceEducation.value: High literacy and reading culture; the University of Iceland (1911); deCODE genetics studies the population’s genealogy.

openness.value: Open to trade and tourism; protective of its fishing grounds.

communicationTransport.value: Ring Road (Route 1) circles the island; no railways; domestic flights and ferries.

religion.value: Mostly Lutheran (Church of Iceland), with a growing non-religious share; Christianity adopted by the Althing in 1000.

languageWriting.value: Icelandic, very close to Old Norse; people use patronymic names (e.g. Jónsdóttir, “daughter of Jón”).

artsArchitecture.value: The medieval sagas, modern music (Björk, Sigur Rós) and turf houses.

socialStructure.value: A small, close-knit society with a large middle class; many people are related.

sharedIdentity.value: Strong identity through language and sagas.

dailyLife.value: Houses heated by hot water; fish, lamb, skyr.

neighbours.value: Greenland, the Faroe Islands, Norway and the UK across the sea.

ideasReligions.value: Norse heritage; early adopter of women’s rights (first elected woman president, Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, 1980).

colonisation.value: Under Norway (1262) and then Denmark until home rule (1918) and full independence (1944).

riseSignals.value: Sovereign kingdom in union with Denmark (1918); republic (1944).

peakPeriod.value: Banking boom of the 2000s, followed by recovery and a tourism boom after 2010.

declineSignals.value: Its three big banks collapsed in the 2008 financial crisis.
